title: Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, finds evidence of DRAM collusion plausible after 500% price surge — says chipmakers acted like ‘hawks flying in formation
summary: Judge denies motion to dismiss DRAM price-fixing lawsuit against major memory makers
detailed: Judge Noël Wise denied a motion to dismiss a DRAM price-fixing class-action lawsuit filed by 17 individuals and small businesses against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix.
The plaintiffs allege that the memory chip makers coordinated parallel supply restrictions, including simultaneous production cuts and a pivot to HBM, causing prices to surge up to 500% in one year.
The defendants argued their actions were independent business responses to market pressures in a concentrated industry, which the judge rejected as plausible collusion.
The court order requires the defendants to respond to the original complaint by December 7, with a case management conference scheduled for January 2027.
This ruling matters because it allows antitrust claims against major memory manufacturers to proceed toward evidence discovery.
sentences: Judge Noël Wise, who presides over the proposed class-action lawsuit against Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix, has denied the companies’ motion to have the case dismissed.

According to the decision, the defendants’ argument that the legal action is just “a rerun” of the same antitrust case filed against the industry in 2018 was rejected as the plaintiffs have established that there’s some new evidence suggesting that there was collusion between the big three memory chip manufacturers.
Micron, Samsung, and SK hynix argued that they watch each other like hawks because of how tight competition is.
Judge Wise disagreed with this characterization, though, saying that what they are accused of goes beyond that.

“Their contentions are more akin to hawks flying in formation — an activity that hawks ordinarily do not do.”
The plaintiffs, which are made up of 17 individuals and small businesses, allege that the companies made four parallel moves that restricted DRAM supply and led to the current shortage, which saw prices jump by as much as 500% in one year.
Despite their rebuttals, the judge decided that the case is plausible enough to move forward.
This isn’t a judgment, though — both sides would still have to show their evidence and speak their arguments before the court before getting a decision.

Because of this, the three companies are given until December 7 to respond to the original complaint with the case management conference, which will determine the administrative matters on the case, set for January 2027.
